scope_conditions.task: multi-hop-QA with adversarial evidence and perturbation stress tests

evidence_gap: There is almost no negative or robustness evidence showing whether planning remains beneficial when retrieval is noisy, contradictory, or partially wrong.

hypothesis: GPT-4 may have genuine but narrow planning ability that appears negative overall because current evidence samples only a few reasoning-style tasks and not broader planning settings.
mechanism: Performance is highly task-structured: GPT-4 variants may succeed on text-based decomposition or multi-step plan synthesis but fail on visuospatial shortest-path or execution-coupled tasks, making one-sided negative evidence look broader than it is.
predictions: gpt-4-turbo-0409 beats gpt-4o on text-only plan synthesis
both models underperform on visual shortest-path variants
minimal_test: Run a preregistered benchmark suite with the same GPT-4 variants (at minimum gpt-4-turbo-0409 and GPT-4o) across matched planning conditions: text-only symbolic planning, grid shortest-path, plan-execution separation, and multimodal spatial planning. Use identical prompts, fixed decoding settings, and at least one non-GPT planning baseline. Report full per-task accuracy, not just aggregated scores, plus negative controls where problem statements are paraphrased without changing graph structure. This would show whether failures are confined to specific modalities/task forms or generalize across planning.

scope_conditions.method: GPT-4 variants compared under identical prompting and decoding
scope_conditions.task: planning split into text-only symbolic, execution-linked, and visuospatial shortest-path settings

evidence_gap: There is no broad, modality-controlled benchmark showing whether GPT-4 planning failures persist outside the few reported reasoning examples or whether any positive performance exists in other planning subtypes.

hypothesis: The apparent lack of positive evidence may be an artifact of selective reporting, with easy or successful planning cases omitted because papers emphasize surprising failures or relative comparisons.
mechanism: When impact_balance is one-sided and only mixed/negative claims are visible, publication and figure-selection incentives can overrepresent implausible-response examples and underreport routine successes, especially without dataset-wide statistics.
predictions: reported examples contain more failure cases than random samples
full-instance accuracy is less negative than showcased examples imply
minimal_test: Obtain or recreate the exact evaluation sets underlying the shortest-path and planning comparisons, then publish complete instance-level outputs for GPT-4o and gpt-4-turbo-0409 on all items, including unsuccessful and successful cases. Include a random-sample audit of prompts not selected by authors, confidence intervals over the full set, and a negative control where item order and visual layout are randomized while shortest-path length is preserved. If aggregate results remain strongly negative across the full unreduced set, selective reporting is less plausible; if showcased failures are much worse than the average, the current picture is biased.

scope_conditions.method: same named models from the claims with original prompts or exact reconstructions
scope_conditions.task: the reported planning/shortest-path evaluations at full dataset level rather than cherry-picked examples

evidence_gap: Current claims do not provide complete dataset-wide distributions, random-sample audits, or full output logs needed to rule out file-drawer or example-selection bias.

hypothesis: GPT-4 planning failures may mostly reflect untested interface and prompt factors rather than a stable inability, so robustness is unknown until adversarial and supportive prompting conditions are both measured.
mechanism: Planning performance can depend on representation format, instruction scaffolding, and whether the model is asked for intermediate state tracking; without controlled ablations, observed negatives may conflate model limits with brittle prompting.
predictions: state-tracking prompts improve shortest-path accuracy
format perturbations cause large accuracy swings
minimal_test: Evaluate GPT-4o and gpt-4-turbo-0409 on the same planning items under a factorial design: direct answer vs chain-of-thought-style decomposition, explicit graph extraction vs raw problem statement, text rendering vs image rendering of the same graph, and with/without self-check instructions. Add adversarial perturbations that preserve the correct answer: node renaming, edge-order shuffling, distractor edges, and paraphrased instructions. Include a negative control of non-planning factual QA prompts matched for length. The exact closing evidence is a robustness table showing whether planning accuracy is stable across these prompt/interface conditions or collapses under benign reformulations.

scope_conditions.method: GPT-4o and gpt-4-turbo-0409 under controlled prompt and modality ablations
scope_conditions.task: planning tasks with answer-preserving representation and instruction perturbations

evidence_gap: No controlled ablation evidence shows whether the reported planning deficits are robust to prompt, modality, and representation changes, or whether positive results emerge with minimal scaffolding.

hypothesis: GPT-4 may have real but narrow commonsense-reasoning ability that fails on distribution-shifted or narrative-heavy benchmarks, so the current negative picture overgeneralizes from hard settings.
mechanism: Performance depends on benchmark construction: GPT-4 may handle standard everyday commonsense cues but break when tasks require story tracking, altered answer priors, or paraphrased worlds as in AIW variants and TiMoS.
predictions: Higher accuracy on original AIW than AIW Ext/Friends
Near-random TiMoS accuracy but above-chance standard commonsense QA
minimal_test: Run GPT-4 on a matched benchmark suite spanning original AIW, AIW Ext, AIW Friends, TiMoS, and at least two standard commonsense-reasoning datasets with identical prompting, decoding, scoring, and contamination checks; report per-item accuracy, calibration, and variance across 5 prompt templates, plus human and random baselines. The gap closes if GPT-4 is shown either consistently above chance across non-narrative commonsense tasks or broadly weak across both original and shifted settings under the same protocol.

scope_conditions.method: GPT-4 with fixed inference settings and prompt templates
scope_conditions.task: commonsense-reasoning including original, variant, and narrative benchmarks

evidence_gap: There is no unified positive-side evaluation showing whether failures on AIW variants and TiMoS generalize to standard commonsense benchmarks under controlled conditions.

hypothesis: The apparent weakness of GPT-4 on commonsense-reasoning could be partly an artifact of benchmark-specific scoring and prompt sensitivity rather than a stable capability deficit.
mechanism: Small changes in instruction wording, answer format constraints, or scorer assumptions can move LLM accuracy sharply; if only one prompt/scoring pipeline was used, negative results may reflect brittle evaluation rather than true inability.
predictions: Accuracy varies materially across prompt paraphrases
Free-form rationale scoring outperforms strict answer-only scoring
minimal_test: For AIW original/Ext/Friends and TiMoS, evaluate GPT-4 with a preregistered prompt grid: zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought hidden, chain-of-thought exposed, answer-only, and schema-constrained output; use both exact-match scoring and blinded human adjudication on a stratified sample of at least 200 items per dataset. Include negative controls where answer labels are shuffled and where prompts contain irrelevant distractor instructions. The gap closes if poor performance persists across prompt/scoring variants and controls, or if performance recovers strongly under robust scoring.

scope_conditions.method: GPT-4 across multiple prompting and scoring protocols
scope_conditions.task: commonsense-reasoning benchmarks with discrete-answer and narrative formats

evidence_gap: Missing are prompt-robustness and scorer-robustness tests, along with negative controls that would distinguish genuine reasoning failure from evaluation artifacts.

hypothesis: The literature may be showing a file-drawer or under-sampled-settings effect, where only difficult commonsense-reasoning cases for GPT-4 are reported and positive effectiveness evidence in easier or practically relevant settings is absent.
mechanism: With low impact balance and no positive claims in the current graph, the visible evidence could be skewed toward failure cases, especially if researchers preferentially publish challenging new datasets without matched broad baselines.
predictions: Published benchmarks overrepresent adversarial/novel settings
Unpublished or omitted standard-task runs show higher GPT-4 accuracy
minimal_test: Conduct a systematic evidence audit for GPT-4 on commonsense-reasoning: collect all papers, appendices, model cards, benchmark leaderboards, and released evaluation scripts from the same time window; extract every GPT-4 result on standard and adversarial commonsense tasks, including null or omitted runs. Then run a registered multi-benchmark replication on both easy and hard datasets with the authors' prompts where available. The gap closes if the audit finds balanced positive evidence on standard tasks, or alternatively confirms that only hard-setting evidence exists and replicates the negative pattern.

scope_conditions.method: GPT-4 evidence synthesis plus direct replication
scope_conditions.task: commonsense-reasoning across standard, adversarial, and narrative datasets

evidence_gap: What is missing is a publication-bias-resistant inventory of GPT-4 commonsense results and a matched replication set spanning both standard and adversarial datasets.

hypothesis: The reported weakness of Llama on multi-step-reasoning is real for small and instruction-tuned variants, but the current evidence is too narrow to justify a general claim about all Llama-family models.
mechanism: Observed failures may be driven by model-scale and variant choice: the cited evidence is concentrated on 8B/7B chat or instruct models and one CodeLlama variant, which may underperform on compositional reasoning relative to larger or differently tuned Llama models.
predictions: Larger Llama variants outperform 7B/8B on the same tasks.
Performance gaps shrink after controlling for prompt format across variants.
minimal_test: Run a preregistered cross-scale benchmark on the same multi-step-reasoning tasks represented by FRoG, board-state rule execution, and StrucText-Eval, evaluating at least three Llama sizes/variants (e.g., 8B, 70B, and a reasoning-tuned Llama if available) under identical prompts, decoding settings, and token budgets; report full accuracy/error-type matrices and compare against one non-Llama model family as a calibration baseline.

scope_conditions.method: Llama variants across scale and tuning, not only 7B/8B chat/instruct or CodeLlama
scope_conditions.task: multi-step-reasoning spanning symbolic rule execution, fuzzy/precise reasoning, and structured text reasoning

evidence_gap: Missing are same-task, same-prompt comparisons across multiple Llama scales and tunings; current claims sample only a few models and do not test whether the negative effect generalizes across the family.

hypothesis: Some of the negative evidence is an artifact of task-format mismatch rather than a core inability in multi-step reasoning, because the tested settings may reward exact state tracking or formatting skills that were not isolated from reasoning ability.
mechanism: Llama models may fail when tasks require strict output schemas, board-state serialization, or LaTeX syntax fidelity; these interface demands can depress measured reasoning performance even if latent stepwise reasoning is better than the headline scores suggest.
predictions: Constrained-output decoding improves board-state and LaTeX task scores.
Reasoning traces are more accurate than final formatted answers on the same items.
minimal_test: For the exact tasks behind the cited claims, rerun Llama with three output conditions: free-form generation, schema-constrained generation (JSON/table/cell-level board updates or LaTeX slot filling), and answer-only multiple-choice/executable verification where formatting burden is removed; include negative controls where the same reasoning content is reformatted into simpler I/O, then score both intermediate reasoning traces and final answers item-by-item.

scope_conditions.method: Llama under free-form versus constrained-output prompting/decoding
scope_conditions.task: multi-step-reasoning tasks with heavy formatting or state-representation requirements

evidence_gap: Missing are ablations that separate reasoning competence from output-format compliance, plus negative controls that hold reasoning constant while changing only representation and scoring interface.

hypothesis: The one-sided negative literature may partly reflect selective reporting and under-testing of favorable prompting/tool conditions, so the apparent lack of positive effectiveness evidence may be exaggerated.
mechanism: With impact_balance and citation-bridge signals both low, published evidence may overrepresent failure cases while omitting settings such as few-shot decomposition, self-verification, external scratchpads, or retrieval-free prompt optimization that could improve Llama on some multi-step tasks.
predictions: Prompting with decomposition yields gains on at least one cited benchmark.
Unpublished or omitted prompt settings show higher variance than reported headline results.
minimal_test: Conduct a registered benchmark sweep on the cited task types using a fixed Llama model set and exhaustively enumerate prompting conditions that are often selectively tuned: zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought, decomposition, self-critique, majority-vote sampling, and scratchpad/no-scratchpad; publish all runs including null results, plus an adversarial split with distractor context and longer reasoning depth to test whether any gains are robust or merely prompt-sensitive.

scope_conditions.method: Llama with and without prompt engineering or lightweight reasoning scaffolds
scope_conditions.task: multi-step-reasoning under both standard and adversarially deeper settings

evidence_gap: Missing are comprehensive all-results-reported sweeps over prompting/scaffolding conditions, as well as adversarial depth and distractor tests that would show whether any positive setting is robust rather than cherry-picked.

hypothesis: The contradiction is driven by dataset composition: multimodal helps on text-lite or symbol-grounded items but hurts on vision-dominant, noisy, or perception-heavy items, so aggregate rankings flip when the benchmark mixes these subsets differently.
mechanism: Benchmarks differ in the proportion of text-dominant versus figure-dependent problems, clean rendered diagrams versus real/noisy images, and recognition versus full reasoning demands; models can look strong when most items are solvable from text or icons, yet weak when success depends on precise spatial perception or counting from images.
predictions: Performance advantage becomes positive on text-lite/icon subsets.
Performance advantage becomes negative on figure-heavy/noisy subsets.
minimal_test: Construct a common evaluation pool stratified into text-dominant, text-lite, vision-dominant, icon-recognition, and real-image/noisy subsets; evaluate the same multimodal and text-only-capable models with identical prompts and scoring, then compare whether the reported contradiction disappears within each fixed stratum.

scope_conditions.task: math-reasoning

evidence_gap: Most claims report pooled benchmark numbers without a shared item taxonomy linking visual load, noise level, and reasoning subtype across datasets.

hypothesis: The disagreement is caused by prompt format and interface choices: multimodal models benefit when the prompt decomposes perception and reasoning or uses structured chain-of-thought/pointing, but can underperform with direct-answer or poorly grounded prompts.
mechanism: Prompt scaffolds change whether the model first extracts visual variables, localizes regions, and then reasons, versus attempting end-to-end inference from raw images; structured prompts and active visual referencing reduce grounding errors, while unstructured prompts expose perception bottlenecks and consistency failures.
predictions: Structured grounding prompts increase accuracy on the same items.
Prompt gains are largest on visually grounded reasoning, not pure text-only items.
minimal_test: Take one shared benchmark and run the same models under two fixed prompt regimes: a minimal direct-answer prompt and a structured prompt with explicit visual extraction/step decomposition or pointing support; keep images, models, decoding, and scoring fixed, and test whether the contradiction across papers collapses under the same prompt regime.

scope_conditions.task: math-reasoning

evidence_gap: Cross-paper comparisons rarely control for hidden prompt templates, tool-use permissions, or whether pointing/structured CoT was enabled at inference.

hypothesis: The apparent conflict arises from evaluation protocol differences: lenient answer matching and average-case scoring make multimodal systems look competitive, whereas strict exact-match, consistency checks, robustness perturbations, or human baselines make them look weak.
mechanism: A model may often produce approximately correct or partially correct outputs that count under loose scoring but fail under strict parsing, multi-step consistency, or perturbation-based robustness tests; changing the protocol can therefore flip a result from positive relative improvement to negative limitation.
predictions: Loose metrics narrow or reverse reported deficits.
Strict/robustness metrics enlarge deficits on the same outputs.
minimal_test: Re-score identical model outputs from the disputed benchmarks under a unified protocol including exact match, loose match, strict consistency, and robustness-perturbed accuracy, while keeping model, data, and prompts fixed; check whether papers that disagree converge once the same scoring protocol is applied.

scope_conditions.task: math-reasoning

evidence_gap: The claims mix benchmark-specific metrics such as Accuracy, worst-case accuracy, strict accuracy, loose score, and human-relative comparisons, but few papers provide cross-metric rescoring on shared outputs.

hypothesis: Agent-based planning appears beneficial on low-branching or well-structured planning instances but can underperform once task composition increases branching factor, partial observability, or physical interaction complexity.
mechanism: Dataset composition moderates the effect: many positive papers evaluate structured domains with explicit state summaries, short horizons, or decomposable subgoals, while negative papers include richer object interactions, hidden state, or harder combinatorics that push agents from plan synthesis into repeated local repair, flipping gains into failures.
predictions: Performance gap is positive on low-complexity splits but shrinks or reverses on high-complexity splits.
Matching papers on horizon and observability removes much of the contradiction.
minimal_test: Construct a shared benchmark stratified by planning complexity variables already implicated in the claims (number of entities, horizon length, observability, interaction richness). Evaluate the same agent method and baseline on each stratum, then compare effect signs after reweighting both papers' reported results to the same complexity distribution.

scope_conditions.task: planning

evidence_gap: Current claims rarely report a harmonized difficulty profile or per-stratum effect sizes across domains, so it is unclear whether disagreement reflects average-case differences or true method instability.

hypothesis: The contradiction is driven by prompt/interface format: agents look strong when given explicit structured state representations, distance tables, experience memories, or inter-agent critique, but weak when acting from underspecified natural-language or ambiguous environment descriptions.
mechanism: Prompt format changes the effective observability and action grounding available to the planner. Structured prompts reduce search and representation burden, enabling better action selection; free-form or weakly grounded prompts leave the model to infer latent state, causing local reasoning errors, implausible actions, and poor plan validity.
predictions: Adding explicit state tables or action constraints improves the weak settings disproportionately.
Removing structured scaffolds from strong settings reduces or reverses the reported advantage.
minimal_test: Take one positive setup and one negative setup, then cross-swap only the interface: run the same backend model and agent loop with (a) structured state/action tables and memory scaffolds and (b) plain natural-language descriptions. If the contradiction is due to prompt/interface format, effect signs should converge under the matched prompt condition.

scope_conditions.task: planning

evidence_gap: Most papers do not release token-level prompts or equivalent state encodings, making it hard to isolate whether the agent algorithm or the interface specification caused the observed gains.

hypothesis: Reported disagreement may flip because different papers use different model scales/backbones and decoding settings, and agent planning benefits emerge only above a capability threshold while smaller or differently decoded models expose failure modes.
mechanism: Model scale and decoding strategy moderate plan quality: larger backbones can maintain longer latent state and better follow multi-step constraints, whereas smaller models or higher-variance decoding produce inconsistent subplans, lower recall, and more correction loops. Thus the same agent design can look excellent with GPT-4-class models and poor with weaker or differently sampled models.
predictions: Under a fixed strong backbone and greedy decoding, cross-paper performance differences narrow.
Replacing strong backbones with smaller ones reproduces more of the negative findings.
minimal_test: Re-run representative positive and negative agent pipelines under a controlled matrix of backbones and decoding parameters: same prompts, same task instances, same evaluation, varying only model family/size and decoding (e.g., temperature 0 vs 0.5). Check whether the sign of the agent-vs-baseline effect aligns once backbone and decoding are held fixed.

scope_conditions.task: planning

evidence_gap: Claims often omit full decoding settings and use non-comparable proprietary backbones, so current evidence cannot separate agent design effects from backend capability effects.

hypothesis: The contradiction is partly driven by dataset composition and evidence cleanliness: RAG looks helpful on domain-focused or evidence-aligned benchmarks but harmful on heterogeneous, noisy, or adversarially contaminated evaluation sets.
mechanism: When queries map to a narrow domain with stable terminology and high corpus-answer overlap, retrieval raises useful evidence recall and improves scoring; when benchmarks include noisy, incomplete, heterogeneous, or poisoned evidence, retrieval injects distractors that can override previously correct parametric knowledge and flip net gains to net losses.
predictions: RAG gains are positive on homogeneous subsets and shrink or turn negative on noisy/heterogeneous subsets
After matching evidence quality across papers, reported effect directions move toward agreement
minimal_test: Build a shared evaluation split stratified by evidence quality/composition (homogeneous high-overlap, heterogeneous, incomplete/noisy, adversarially contaminated). Run the same RAG pipeline and no-retrieval baseline on each stratum with identical corpus, retriever, generator, and prompts. Check whether positive papers' gains concentrate in the high-overlap stratum and negative papers' losses concentrate in noisy/heterogeneous strata; then reweight each paper to the same stratum proportions and test whether the contradiction disappears.

scope_conditions.task: evaluation

evidence_gap: Most claims do not report the proportion of noisy, adversarial, or heterogeneous items, so cross-paper effect estimates cannot yet be normalized by evidence composition.

hypothesis: The disagreement is caused by retrieval operating point differences—especially top-k, ranking precision, and document ordering—so papers are measuring different points on a non-monotonic recall-vs-distraction curve.
mechanism: RAG often helps when a small high-precision set is retrieved, but adding more documents, reversing order, or using lower-precision rankings increases irrelevant context and attention competition; this can turn retrieval from beneficial to harmful even for the same model and task.
predictions: Performance peaks at a small top-k and declines when extra low-precision documents are added
Controlling document order and retrieved-set size reduces cross-paper disagreement
minimal_test: Take one shared benchmark and corpus, then rerun the compared RAG methods under a common retrieval protocol: same retriever, same chunking, same reranker, fixed top-k grid, and fixed presentation order (sequential only). Measure answer quality as k increases and under reversed order. If papers that reported gains were operating near the precision-optimal k while negative papers used larger or differently ordered contexts, harmonizing these settings should collapse the contradiction.

scope_conditions.task: evaluation

evidence_gap: Many papers omit exact retrieved-set sizes, ranking thresholds, or context ordering, making it unclear whether they compared equivalent retrieval operating points.

hypothesis: The apparent conflict reflects generator-scale and prompting/evaluation-protocol interactions: smaller or weaker generators benefit more from retrieval, while stronger generators under different prompts or scoring rules can see little gain or even regression.
mechanism: Retrieval substitutes for missing parametric knowledge in smaller models and under tasks needing explicit citation support, but large models may already answer well without retrieval and become more sensitive to prompt framing, retrieved-context formatting, or judge metrics that penalize redundancy, privacy leakage, or trustworthiness failures. Changing model scale or evaluation rubric can therefore flip the sign of the measured RAG effect.
predictions: RAG gains are larger for smaller backbones under a fixed prompt and metric
Using one shared prompt template and one shared scoring rubric narrows sign differences across model families
minimal_test: Select two model scales (small and large) and evaluate RAG vs no-RAG on the same benchmark using a single prompt template, identical retrieved context formatting, and a unified evaluation protocol that reports both task accuracy and trustworthiness-style penalties. Then swap only model scale while holding everything else fixed. If the contradiction is moderator-driven, the sign or magnitude of the RAG effect should differ systematically by scale and shrink when prompt and scoring are standardized.

scope_conditions.task: evaluation

evidence_gap: Cross-paper reports rarely isolate model scale from prompt design and metric choice, so it remains unclear whether negative findings come from the retriever itself or from generator/rubric interactions.

hypothesis: The contradiction is moderated by task grounding demands: multimodal helps when the agentic task mainly requires semantic interpretation or high-level planning, but hurts when success depends on precise pixel- or geometry-level action grounding.
mechanism: Vision-language inputs add useful context for instruction understanding, navigation intent, and behavior reasoning, yet current multimodal stacks can still fail at exact localization, click-point selection, grasp pose mapping, or fine scene-relation grounding; this can flip results depending on whether the benchmark rewards semantic choice versus low-level actuation accuracy.
predictions: Benefits shrink on pixel-grounded GUI or grasp-localization subsets
Benefits grow on high-level decision or long-horizon planning subsets
minimal_test: Take one shared multimodal agent architecture and evaluate it on a benchmark split explicitly partitioned into semantic-planning items versus precise-grounding items, with the same model, prompts, and decoding. If the moderator is correct, the positive and negative papers' gap should largely disappear after matching for grounding-demand stratum.

scope_conditions.task: agentic-reasoning

evidence_gap: Few claims report matched evaluations that isolate semantic reasoning from low-level grounding error within the same environment and model.

hypothesis: The contradiction is moderated by input distribution and environment composition: multimodal appears beneficial on cleaner or structured environments, but its advantage can reverse under heterogeneous interfaces, accents, corruptions, unseen layouts, or deployment-specific shifts.
mechanism: Multimodal agents often rely on brittle perception modules whose error rate rises under resolution variation, diverse GUI elements, speech accents, aerial viewpoints, real-world clutter, or corrupted driving scenes; papers using more controlled distributions report gains, while papers emphasizing harder shifts report limitations or mixed results.
predictions: Performance drops most on unseen or heterogeneous-interface splits
Contradiction weakens after reweighting papers to a common distribution
minimal_test: Construct a common evaluation suite with matched in-distribution and shifted splits (e.g., seen/unseen layouts, clean/corrupted visuals, standard/accented speech, homogeneous/heterogeneous GUI elements) and run the same multimodal agent variants from both sides. Then compare effects within each split; if distribution is the moderator, sign disagreement should shrink when both are tested on the same composition.

scope_conditions.task: agentic-reasoning

evidence_gap: The current claims rarely quantify shift severity in a directly comparable way across GUI, robotics, navigation, and driving settings.

hypothesis: The contradiction is moderated by evaluation protocol and prompting: multimodal looks strong under module-assisted or constrained-response protocols, but weaker under end-to-end free-form evaluation with stricter success criteria.
mechanism: Several positive results use auxiliary detectors, spatial prompts, depth experts, visual grounding modules, or binary/closed-form outputs, which reduce generation ambiguity and offload perception; negative results often describe direct end-to-end agent use where a single multimodal model must perceive, reason, and act without scaffolding. Different success metrics (binary detection, SR/SPL, full task completion) can therefore flip the sign.
predictions: Module-assisted prompts outperform direct end-to-end prompts on the same tasks
Sign disagreement shrinks under a unified success metric and output format
minimal_test: Re-run a shared benchmark with one model under two controlled conditions: (1) direct end-to-end prompting with open-form action outputs, and (2) the same model plus the exact auxiliary scaffolds used in positive papers, with identical data and decoding. Score both using one harmonized metric such as full task success plus grounding accuracy. If protocol is the moderator, the contradiction should attenuate once prompting and scoring are standardized.

scope_conditions.task: agentic-reasoning

evidence_gap: Cross-paper reports usually do not ablate scaffolding, output constraints, and metric choice simultaneously on identical tasks.

hypothesis: Prompting gains in agentic-reasoning flip sign depending on task composition, with prompts helping multi-step, constraint-heavy tasks but hurting or saturating on simple single-step or single-parameter tasks.
mechanism: Structured or reasoning-augmented prompts add planning scaffolds that improve decomposition and state tracking when tasks require multiple dependent decisions; the same scaffolds add unnecessary verbosity or distraction on simple tasks, where direct prompting or standard function calling is already sufficient.
predictions: Prompt advantage grows with task depth and parameter count.
On single-parameter tasks, direct prompts match or beat reasoning prompts.
minimal_test: Create a shared evaluation slice that bins the same benchmark instances by compositional difficulty (single-step/single-parameter vs multi-step/multi-constraint). Run the same prompted and baseline methods with identical models and decoding on each bin; the contradiction should shrink if both papers are compared within the same difficulty bin rather than on aggregate.

scope_conditions.task: agentic-reasoning

evidence_gap: Most claims report overall averages without matched difficulty strata or per-instance complexity annotations, so it is unclear whether opposite findings come from different mixes of easy and hard agent tasks.

hypothesis: The contradiction is moderated by prompt format and action serialization, with prompts that align to the environment's required schema or state representation helping, while free-form or overconstrained natural-language prompts reduce execution accuracy.
mechanism: Agentic systems are sensitive to whether the prompt elicits outputs in code, JSON, templated function calls, interleaved state-action format, or unconstrained prose. Schema-aligned formats reduce syntax and argument errors, but mismatched or workflow-prescriptive formats can constrain exploration, trigger unintended corrections, or degrade argument generation.
predictions: Schema-aligned prompts improve syntax and argument accuracy.
Free-form or rigid workflow prompts hurt tool-call correctness on the same tasks.
minimal_test: On one common tool-use benchmark, keep model, tools, and examples fixed while varying only output format/instructions across free-form NL, templated NL, JSON/schema-constrained, and code-style prompting. Evaluate exact execution, argument accuracy, and tool selection; if format is the moderator, papers that disagree should converge when compared under the same serialization format.

scope_conditions.task: agentic-reasoning

evidence_gap: Several papers compare different prompt families but do not normalize action grammar, parser strictness, or whether outputs are executed as code, JSON, or text, leaving format as an unmeasured confounder.

hypothesis: Model scale and decoding strategy jointly moderate the effect of prompting, so prompting appears beneficial in some papers because it is tested on smaller or deterministic settings, but weak or harmful in others using larger models or higher-temperature sampling.
mechanism: Smaller models often benefit more from explicit reasoning or templates because prompts compensate for weaker internal planning, whereas larger models may already internalize the structure and can be overconstrained. Higher temperature increases trajectory variance and can wash out prompt gains, especially in long-horizon agents where early stochastic errors compound.
predictions: Prompt gains are larger for 7B-8B models than frontier models.
Raising temperature reduces or reverses prompt gains on agent tasks.
minimal_test: Evaluate the same prompting intervention on a controlled model ladder (e.g., 8B, 32B, 70B/proprietary frontier) at fixed temperatures 0.0 and 0.7 with identical benchmarks and prompts. Then compare prompted-minus-baseline deltas within each scale/temperature cell; if this moderator is responsible, conflicting papers should agree once matched on both model scale and decoding.

scope_conditions.task: agentic-reasoning

evidence_gap: Many reported results mix model families and sampling settings or omit full decoding details, making it hard to separate true prompt effects from scale-dependent and stochasticity-dependent interactions.

hypothesis: The sign of chain-of-thought effects flips with dataset composition, especially whether the benchmark primarily tests sequential compositional reasoning versus perception-heavy, non-sequential, or structure-grounding subtasks.
mechanism: CoT helps when latent solution paths can be decomposed into ordered symbolic subproblems, but harms when the bottleneck is perceptual grounding, non-sequential search, or parsing structured inputs; extra verbal steps then amplify early perceptual/parsing errors instead of adding useful computation.
predictions: CoT gains are positive on sequential symbolic subsets and negative on perceptual/non-sequential subsets.
Within one benchmark, stratifying by operation variety or structure type shrinks the contradiction.
minimal_test: Build a shared evaluation slice across the cited benchmarks with matched model and prompt, then partition examples into sequential-symbolic, non-sequential, perceptual-grounding, and structure-rich categories. Re-run direct prompting and CoT on each partition; the contradiction should largely disappear after comparing only matched partitions rather than benchmark-level averages.

scope_conditions.task: multi-step-reasoning

evidence_gap: Most papers report aggregate scores but do not normalize task mixture or annotate examples by decomposition type, grounding load, or structure complexity.

hypothesis: The contradiction is driven by prompt format differences: CoT helps when the prompt enforces concise, task-aligned step decomposition or demonstrations, but hurts when generic zero-shot phrases induce verbosity, boundary confusion, or unsafe formatting.
mechanism: Prompt wording changes the internal search policy and output format. Demonstration-based or constrained step prompts can scaffold decomposition, whereas generic prompts like 'Let's think step by step' may trigger long, unstructured reasoning, answer leakage, safeguard triggers, or confusion about where rationale ends and answer begins.
predictions: Constrained CoT templates outperform generic zero-shot CoT on the same examples.
Formatting the final answer separately removes much of the reported CoT drop.
minimal_test: Take one positive and one negative benchmark, hold model, decoding, and data fixed, and compare four prompt variants: direct answer, generic zero-shot CoT, demonstration-based CoT, and constrained CoT with explicit answer slot and step limit. If prompt format is the moderator, performance rankings should converge across papers once the same template is used.

scope_conditions.task: multi-step-reasoning

evidence_gap: Cross-paper comparisons rarely use identical templates or report enough prompt details to isolate whether failures come from reasoning itself or from output-format side effects.

hypothesis: Model scale/capability is the moderator: CoT improves stronger models that can use intermediate steps productively, but degrades smaller or weaker multimodal models that generate low-quality rationales.
mechanism: Higher-capacity models can maintain coherent latent state across steps and revise mistakes, so explicit reasoning converts capacity into better answers. Scaling model size while fixing prompt and decoding yields a crossover from negative to positive CoT effect.

Few-shot benefits disappear or flip when the same prompt is rescored with strict normalized answer extraction.

Olympiad/perturbed subsets show negative results

Proof-validity scoring yields smaller or negative gains

Rankings compress under accuracy but spread under loose scoring.

Cross-scoring perturbed items causes larger drops than clean-item rescoring.

scope_conditions.task: planning

evidence_gap: The literature contains many domain-specific failures in physical or partially observable settings, but limited same-benchmark experiments that vary only the explicitness of task type.

hypothesis: The divergence is primarily driven by the retriever choice: stronger or hybrid/domain-matched retrievers make RAG look beneficial, while weaker, mismatched, or sparse-only retrievers make RAG appear neutral or harmful under otherwise fixed evaluation setups.
mechanism: Retriever quality changes the relevance-density of the evidence pool before generation; when the retriever is well matched, retrieved passages increase answer support, but when it is mismatched they inject distractors that overwrite correct parametric answers or reduce precision.

Replacing a weak retriever with a stronger one flips some negative RAG deltas to positive.
minimal_test: On MIRAGE or HotpotQA-style evaluation, keep generator, prompt, top_k, chunking, and context_length fixed; sweep only retriever over BM25, Contriever, dense domain-tuned, and hybrid fusion (e.g., RRF-2/RRF-4), then compare RAG-vs-no-RAG delta and retrieval precision/answer accuracy.

scope_conditions.task: multi-hop-QA

hypothesis: The divergence is primarily driven by retriever choice: tool-use appears beneficial when a stronger or dependency-aware retriever is used, but weak or mismatched retrievers can erase or reverse the gain on agentic-reasoning benchmarks.

scope_conditions.task: agentic-reasoning

evidence_gap: Few claims isolate retrieval while holding prompt formatting, tool presentation, and downstream execution policy constant across the same benchmark.

hypothesis: The responsible setting is top_k: conflicting papers may be evaluating the same tool-use method at different candidate-set sizes, with too-small k missing needed tools and too-large k adding distractors that reduce precision.
mechanism: top_k directly trades off recall against distraction load; low k truncates away required tools or dependencies, while higher k improves recall up to a plateau and then can burden the model with more near-miss tools, changing whether tool-use helps overall.
predictions: On BFCL, success improves from k=1 to a small intermediate k, then plateaus or drops at larger k.
On MCP tool selection, hit rate rises sharply by k=3 while latency changes little under the same system.
minimal_test: On BFCL or the 121-tool MCP benchmark, keep retriever, model, prompt, and context budget fixed; sweep only top_k across {1,3,5,10,20,30,50} and report tool recall/precision plus end-to-end task success.

scope_conditions.task: agentic-reasoning

evidence_gap: Existing reports often vary k together with reranking, pruning, or optimization methods, so the k-only causal contribution remains under-identified.

hypothesis: The divergence is caused by context_length: tool-use helps in shorter or cleaner contexts but degrades in long-context or distractor-heavy settings where tool specifications and responses exceed the model’s effective working memory.
mechanism: As context grows, the model must search over more tool descriptions, prior turns, and tool outputs; this increases position sensitivity, distractor interference, and schema confusion, which can turn a positive tool-use effect into lower accuracy or premature stopping.
predictions: On ToolHaystack, accuracy falls as distractors or retained history increase under the same agent.
On long-context function-calling benchmarks, enlarging tool catalogs to 65k-120k-equivalent context lowers success for most models with fixed retrieval and prompting.
minimal_test: On ToolHaystack or the long-context function-calling benchmark, hold model, retriever, top_k, and task type fixed; sweep only context_length by varying retained history or total tool-catalog/response tokens (e.g., 10K, 20K, 40K, 80K, 120K) and measure accuracy plus stop_early and hallucination rates.

scope_conditions.task: agentic-reasoning

evidence_gap: Cross-paper comparisons mix long context with different distractor constructions and model families, leaving unclear whether raw context length alone is the flipping variable.

hypothesis: The reported divergence is primarily driven by the top_k cutoff: agentic gains become more visible at larger candidate sets, while small k can erase or reverse the advantage on domain-QA benchmarks.
mechanism: Multi-agent systems often improve reranking, diversification, or error recovery across candidate hypotheses rather than sharpening the very top prediction; when evaluation uses top-1 or top-3, extra agent proposals may look noisy, but at top-5 to top-20 they can recover missed correct answers and flip the measured effect.
predictions: On the CWE benchmark, agent < single-agent at top-1/top-3 but agent > single-agent at top-10/top-20.
The estimated agent gain increases monotonically as k is swept upward on at least one retrieval-style domain-QA benchmark.
minimal_test: Re-run the original single-agent and agent systems on the vulnerable-function CWE identification benchmark from arxiv:2508.01451v1 with all prompts/models/data fixed, sweeping only top_k over {1,3,5,10,20,50}; report recall@k and the sign of agent-minus-single-agent at each k.

scope_conditions.task: domain-QA with ranked candidate outputs or retrieval-style evaluation

evidence_gap: Most claims in the anomaly do not report matched top_k sweeps, so it is unclear whether conflicts come from different cutoffs or from unreported architectural differences.

hypothesis: The responsible setting variable is an effective top_k budget allocated per agent or per round: when k is too small, multi-agent coordination fragments evidence and harms answer quality, but when k is large enough the same method turns beneficial.
mechanism: Agents split exploration across roles or rounds; under a tight k budget each agent sees or proposes too few candidates, causing coverage loss and premature consensus, whereas a larger k restores complementary evidence and allows aggregation to outperform a single-pass baseline.
predictions: With fixed total setup, increasing top_k from very small values will first improve recall/accuracy sharply for the agent variant before plateauing.
The agent variant will be more sensitive to low-k truncation than the single-agent baseline on at least one benchmark.
minimal_test: On the original CWE identification benchmark from arxiv:2508.01451v1, keep model, prompts, and number of agents fixed and sweep only top_k per agent over {1,2,3,5,10,20}; compare agent and single-agent recall@k and measure sensitivity to low-k truncation.

scope_conditions.task: domain-QA where candidate/evidence budget is truncated by k

evidence_gap: The papers rarely specify whether k is global, per-agent, or per-round, so the field may hide an interaction between coordination and candidate-budget granularity.

hypothesis: The divergence is caused by benchmark-specific optimal top_k: some domain-QA tasks favor precision-oriented small k, while others reward coverage-oriented large k, making the same agent method look conflicting across papers that use different k.
mechanism: Agent systems can increase hypothesis diversity and evidence breadth; on tasks scored by exact top answer, extra candidates may dilute precision, but on tasks with recall-style or partial-credit evaluation, broader k improves the chance that one agent surfaces the needed evidence or label.
predictions: A small-k regime will maximize exact-match or top-1 accuracy on some benchmarks, while a larger-k regime will maximize recall-oriented metrics on others.
Holding the agent method fixed, the sign and size of its advantage will vary across benchmarks solely from changing top_k.
minimal_test: Evaluate one original precision-oriented benchmark and one original recall-oriented benchmark from the payload using the same agent setup and a top_k sweep {1,3,5,10,20}; for example, sweep k on the CWE identification benchmark from arxiv:2508.01451v1 and the FIQA-2018 retrieval benchmark from arxiv:2511.14130v2, keeping all non-k settings fixed within each benchmark.

scope_conditions.task: domain-QA across benchmarks with different evaluation targets

evidence_gap: There is little directly comparable reporting of the same agent architecture under identical settings except for k, so cross-benchmark metric sensitivity remains unquantified.

hypothesis: The divergence is driven by task_type switching between answer-generation reasoning tasks and direct evaluation/classification-style tasks.
mechanism: When the same evaluation-method is applied to spatial reasoning, generation-heavy reasoning tasks reward chain-like inference and model/world knowledge, while evaluation-style tasks compress the problem into recognition or choice scoring, changing which models appear strong and whether gains are visible.
predictions: On Spatial-DISE, switching task_type from evaluation to reasoning will increase between-model accuracy spread.
On the same benchmark, some models that are near-tied under evaluation will separate under reasoning prompts.
minimal_test: On Spatial-DISE, hold models, images, metric, and scoring fixed; vary only task_type by running the original items in two modes: evaluation (direct label/choice output) versus reasoning (free-form rationale then answer), and compare ranking changes and accuracy deltas for Qwen2.5-VL-7B and Gemini2.0-Flash.

scope_conditions.task: spatial reasoning

evidence_gap: The papers do not report matched runs where only task_type changes on the same benchmark and model set.

hypothesis: The responsible variable is task_type defined as static single-frame spatial judgment versus dynamic/multi-step spatial reasoning.
mechanism: Dynamic tasks require temporal state tracking and trajectory updates, whereas static tasks rely more on snapshot geometry; this can flip the apparent effect of the evaluation-method because models may benefit from one subtask decomposition but fail on the other.
predictions: Within Spatial-DISE, dynamic items will show larger gains than static items under the same evaluation-method.
On a benchmark split by static vs dynamic spatial items, model rankings will change even with identical prompts and scoring.
minimal_test: On Spatial-DISE, hold model, prompt template, image format, and metric fixed; vary only task_type by evaluating the original static subset and dynamic subset separately, then compare per-model accuracy and ranking shifts under the same evaluation-method.

scope_conditions.task: spatial reasoning

evidence_gap: Current claims compare static and dynamic outcomes but do not isolate whether the evaluation-method itself interacts with this task_type split across the same controlled setup.

hypothesis: The key variable is task_type as difficulty/compositional load, ranging from easy local judgments to hard global or multi-node reasoning.
mechanism: As compositional load rises, the same evaluation-method may stop reflecting true reasoning competence because errors compound over intermediate spatial relations; on easier task types, models can look competitive or above chance, while on harder ones they collapse.
predictions: On MRT, the gap between easy and full-benchmark accuracy will persist when only task_type difficulty is changed.
On BBH Navigate, increasing node-count difficulty within the same task_type family will sharply reduce positive accuracy for most models.
minimal_test: Run a parameter sweep over task_type difficulty on one original benchmark: either MRT Easy to harder MRT subsets, or BBH Navigate with original node-count settings; keep model, prompt, decoding, and metric fixed and measure whether accuracy degrades monotonically as only task_type difficulty increases.

scope_conditions.task: spatial reasoning

evidence_gap: We lack a unified benchmark report that aligns easy and hard spatial task types under one identical evaluation pipeline across the same models.

hypothesis: The setting variable most likely flipping the reported effect of evaluation-method on domain-QA is task_type, with evaluation-style tasks favoring stronger measured gains while reasoning-style tasks suppress or reverse them.
mechanism: Evaluation tasks often compare outputs to references or judge consistency/diversity, which rewards calibration and rubric alignment; reasoning tasks require multi-step inference where the same evaluation method can expose logical failures instead of improvements.
predictions: On a medical QA benchmark, evaluation-mode scores exceed reasoning-mode scores for the same model and prompts.
The advantage of M-Eval over direct evaluation shrinks or disappears when identical items are rewritten as multi-step reasoning questions.
minimal_test: On one original benchmark from arxiv:2510.23995v1 (medical question-answering evaluation) and one reasoning benchmark such as the inheritance law benchmark from arxiv:2509.01081v2, hold model, prompts, decoding, and scoring pipeline fixed; sweep only task_type by evaluating the same answer sets under evaluation vs reasoning-formatted question variants, and compare the effect size of evaluation-method against the same baseline on each benchmark.

scope_conditions.task: domain-QA

evidence_gap: Few claims directly compare the same items under both evaluation and reasoning task formulations while holding all other settings fixed.

hypothesis: The responsible setting variable is top_k, where allowing multiple candidate answers changes apparent effectiveness of evaluation-method by converting failures at top-1 into partial successes at top-3 or top-5.
mechanism: Some domain-QA evaluations credit presence of a correct hypothesis anywhere in the ranked list; methods that seem weak under strict single-answer scoring can look substantially better when the candidate set is expanded, especially in diagnosis-style tasks with broad differential answers.
predictions: Effect sizes are smallest at top-1 and larger at top-3 on the diagnostic benchmark.
Beyond top-3, additional gains from the evaluation method flatten on the same benchmark.
minimal_test: Using the original diagnostic prediction/provisional diagnosis benchmark from arxiv:2510.10278v1, keep model, prompts, dataset split, and scorer fixed; sweep only top_k over {1,2,3,5} and re-evaluate the same outputs under the same evaluation-method and baseline to test whether the sign or magnitude of the claimed advantage changes.

scope_conditions.task: domain-QA

evidence_gap: The conflict set contains only sparse explicit top_k reporting, so we lack direct cross-paper comparisons at matched top_k values.

hypothesis: Task_type is responsible in a more specific way: factual retrieval-style domain-QA tends to produce weaker or negative effects for evaluation-method than evaluation-centric task_type, because factual granularity penalties dominate the measured outcome.
mechanism: In factual tasks, correctness hinges on exact citation/provision/granularity matching, so the evaluation method has less room to show improvement and may instead highlight retrieval or specificity failures; in evaluation-centric tasks, coarse correctness or rubric-based judgments can amplify perceived gains.
predictions: On legal provision QA, the evaluation-method advantage is smaller under factual exact-match than under evaluation-style judging of the same responses.
As item granularity becomes more specific within the same factual benchmark, the measured benefit of evaluation-method declines.
minimal_test: On the statutory recall benchmark from arxiv:2509.21208v1, hold corpus, model, prompts, and answer set fixed; sweep only task_type by scoring the identical responses once as factual exact-match/citation resolution and once as evaluation-style judged correctness, then compare effect sizes across article vs subparagraph subsets.

scope_conditions.task: domain-QA

evidence_gap: There is no direct within-paper ablation that evaluates identical outputs under both factual and evaluation-style task types on the same legal benchmark.

hypothesis: The retriever choice is a primary setting variable that can flip whether RAG helps factual-QA, with stronger or better-matched retrievers turning negative/mixed outcomes into gains while weaker or mismatched retrievers erase them.
mechanism: Retriever quality and match to corpus/query style determine whether the context contains at least one answer-bearing document; when retrieval precision/recall is below a task-dependent threshold, added context injects noise or causes refusal, but when the retriever is better aligned, RAG becomes beneficial.
predictions: Holding top_k and context_length fixed, swapping BM25/e5 for a stronger hybrid or reranked retriever raises answer accuracy on NQ.
Holding top_k and context_length fixed, weak retrievers will keep RAG below no-retrieval on harder sets like TriviaQA.
minimal_test: On NaturalQuestions and TriviaQA, keep the generator, prompt, top_k, and context length fixed; sweep only retriever across BM25, e5, Contriever, hybrid BM25+dense, and hybrid+rereanker, then measure retrieval precision/Recall@1 and end-to-end EM/F1 versus the same no-retrieval baseline.

scope_conditions.task: factual-QA

evidence_gap: Few directly comparable studies report the same generator and prompt with only retriever swapped across the same benchmark plus a no-retrieval control.

hypothesis: The top_k setting is responsible for much of the divergence: too few retrieved documents miss evidence, while too many retrieved documents dilute relevance and can reverse RAG gains.
mechanism: Top_k controls a non-monotonic trade-off between recall and noise. Small k can omit gold evidence; moderate k captures needed support; large k overloads the model with distractors, lowering grounding efficiency and sometimes making RAG worse than smaller-k or no-retrieval runs.
predictions: With retriever and context budget fixed, accuracy on NQ peaks at intermediate k rather than at the maximum k tested.
With retriever and context budget fixed, moving from moderate k to very large k hurts HotpotQA or TriviaQA despite higher retrieval recall.
minimal_test: On NQ and HotpotQA, keep retriever, chunking, prompt, model, and total context formatting fixed; sweep only top_k over {1,3,5,10,20,50,100,150,300,500} and record EM/F1 plus gold-document incidence to locate the turning point where added documents become harmful.

scope_conditions.task: factual-QA

evidence_gap: Most papers compare only a few k values or change reranking/compression jointly, leaving the pure top_k curve undercontrolled.

hypothesis: Context_length is the setting variable that flips outcomes because longer contexts help only when the model can use them effectively; beyond model-specific limits, extra retrieved content increases distraction rather than grounding.
mechanism: Context length determines how much of the retrieved set reaches the generator. For long-context-capable models, larger windows preserve more evidence and improve factuality; for weaker long-context models or poorly ordered contexts, added tokens reduce attention to salient evidence and degrade answer correctness.
predictions: Holding retriever and top_k fixed, recent long-context models improve from short to mid-long windows on NQ.
Holding retriever and top_k fixed, some models plateau or decline once context exceeds their effective long-context range.
minimal_test: On NQ or TriviaQA, keep retriever, retrieved set, document order, and top_k fixed; sweep only context_length over {2k, 4k, 8k, 16k, 32k, 64k, 100k} tokens for at least two original benchmark models, and compare EM/F1 plus evidence utilization rates.

scope_conditions.task: factual-QA

evidence_gap: Existing claims often conflate context length with model choice or document count, so pure window-length ablations on identical retrieved evidence are sparse.

hypothesis: The task_type setting is the primary variable flipping multimodal outcomes: multimodal models look favorable on direct visual factual answering but unfavorable on evidence-localization or cross-page source-attribution variants of factual-QA.
mechanism: Changing only task_type changes the supervision target from answer generation to grounding/localization, which taxes visual alignment and citation skills rather than raw answer production; the same multimodal capacity can therefore help on answering while hurting on attribution-heavy variants.
predictions: On Wiki-VISA, answer-generation accuracy stays higher than bounding-box accuracy when only task_type is switched.
On a shared multimodal model, factual VQA ranking is stronger than evidence-localization ranking under matched inputs.
minimal_test: Using one multimodal model and one benchmark family with paired annotations (e.g., Wiki-VISA), sweep only task_type across answer generation vs bounding box prediction while keeping dataset split, prompt, model, and input images fixed; compare whether the sign of the multimodal advantage changes between task types.

scope_conditions.task: factual-QA with paired answering and grounding annotations

evidence_gap: Current claims mix different models and benchmarks, so there is no within-model, within-dataset ablation isolating task_type alone.

hypothesis: Within task_type, the long-context vs short-context instantiation of factual-QA is the setting variable responsible for divergence: multimodal gains persist on first-page/short-context evidence but collapse when the relevant evidence lies beyond the first page.
mechanism: Holding the model fixed, longer evidence contexts dilute visual-text alignment, increase distractors, and exceed effective cross-modal attention span, so multimodal systems that answer well in compact contexts fail to localize or support answers in long-context settings.
predictions: On Wiki-VISA, accuracy is higher for first-page passages than beyond-first-page passages at fixed model and prompt.
The multimodal advantage shrinks monotonically as task_type is swept from short-context factual-QA to long-context factual-QA.
minimal_test: On Wiki-VISA, hold model, training state, and evaluation metric fixed and sweep only task_type between short-context single-page factual-QA and long-context multi-page factual-QA formulations; measure whether performance drops and whether the direction of multimodal benefit changes across the sweep.

scope_conditions.task: factual-QA where evidence position can be restricted to first page or extended beyond first page

evidence_gap: Existing evidence shows a page-position effect, but not a controlled short-vs-long task_type sweep with all other conditions fixed.

hypothesis: The evaluation-style task_type setting is responsible: multimodal methods appear positive in zero-shot factual answering but negative when task_type switches to transfer/generalization evaluation across datasets.
mechanism: A change from in-domain factual answering to cross-dataset transfer evaluation stresses domain-invariant grounding; multimodal systems may exploit dataset-specific visual-text correlations that boost in-domain scores yet fail under transfer, reversing the apparent effect.
predictions: A multimodal model that is competitive in zero-shot in-domain factual-QA shows a marked drop when evaluated in cross-dataset transfer mode only.
On VISA-style benchmarks, transfer evaluation yields lower multimodal gains than standard in-domain factual evaluation at fixed model size and prompt.
minimal_test: Take one multimodal model and one paired benchmark setup from Wiki-VISA and Paper-VISA; sweep only task_type between standard in-domain factual evaluation and cross-dataset transfer evaluation, keeping architecture, training budget, prompt, and metric fixed, then test whether the sign or magnitude of multimodal advantage changes.

scope_conditions.task: factual-QA with both in-domain and cross-dataset evaluation protocols

evidence_gap: The present claims do not directly compare the same model under in-domain versus transfer evaluation with identical preprocessing and prompts.
